ratings.reason: The quote explicitly describes text and visual inputs fused into one request with flexible switching, nearly matching the structural signature verbatim. Image refinement benefits from the combination, but this is a comparatively settled text-plus-scribble design and the supplied evidence does not establish unusually strong outcomes.

Gesture parameters are explicitly synthesized with speech, making fusion central rather than incidental. Co-speech gesture gives spatial modeling capabilities that speech alone lacks and transfers to other spatial authoring tasks, though the quote does not expose the concrete interaction or reported outcomes.

This is an exceptionally legible fusion mechanism: sketch marks establish referents while simultaneous speech supplies the operation. The examples show how multimodality resolves underspecified commands and are readily transferable beyond debriefing slides.

Gaze, pointing, conversation history, and speech are fused to solve the concrete breakdown of pronoun ambiguity. The design materially extends usable voice interaction in situated environments, although its wearable-AR implementation somewhat limits direct portability.

Images, color, and text explicitly feed one GenAI prompt, cleanly satisfying the pattern. The modality mix improves expressive design exploration and transfers broadly, but multimodal moodboard prompting is now a competent rather than surprising move.

The evidence says modalities can be chosen individually or combined for one onboarding activity, which supports interchangeability, while the title identifies voice, text, and pointing. It does not explain how combined inputs are fused or show that this familiar modality menu changes outcomes.

Vocal instructions and gestures are explicitly interpreted together for object manipulation. This addresses spatial deixis well and transfers to many embodied interfaces, but speech-plus-gesture manipulation is an established multimodal design and the supplied quote lacks interaction detail.

Point-and-click and natural language are two physically distinct methods for the same item-selection operation, supporting interchangeability. Accessibility can make the choice consequential, but the evidence does not show fusion, mid-operation switching, or a particularly novel mechanism.

Combining co-speech gesture with speech is directly on-pattern and likely useful for spatial reference. The quote establishes centrality but gives no example of what gestures mean, how fusion works, or what improvement results, so impact and rebuildability remain uncertain.

The example clearly couples a spoken comparison with pointing that supplies its operands. However, one illustrative scenario provides limited evidence about the implemented capture and arbitration mechanism, and speech-plus-pointing deixis is a canonical rather than field-moving design.

Hands-on shape manipulation and speech jointly convey one generative intent, making modality fusion the authoring method itself. Mapping physical form and language into swarm behavior is unusually inventive, though the swarm hardware and task reduce direct generalizability.

“Co-speech handwriting” suggests simultaneous speech and pen input, but the quote does not say whether they form one fused request or merely coexist in tutoring. The educational use could be consequential, yet the pattern mechanism cannot be judged confidently from the supplied evidence.

Gaze and voice jointly perform physical-object selection, a clean multimodal referencing operation. It plausibly makes displayless glasses more usable, but the sequential “gazeify then voiceify” design and specialized hardware constrain generality, and the quote omits arbitration details.

The agent accepts queries through voice and pen input, but the evidence does not state whether these channels are fused, interchangeable, or used for distinct query types. The embodied pen-and-haptics system is interesting, although much of that novelty lies outside the input pattern.

Sketch and speech are integrated directly over an existing interface for one context-aware LLM interaction. The application-agnostic overlay makes the mechanism unusually transferable, while combining visible UI referents with language offers more than another domain-specific sketch prompt.

Speech, grabbing, and movement are collected together and interpreted by agents, suggesting fused observation of one unfolding play interaction. This is a distinctive alternative to explicit prompting, but the quote does not clarify request boundaries or whether all channels control the same operation.

Facial-expression frames are explicitly combined with message text into one chatbot input, clearly satisfying multi-channel fusion. Nonverbal affect can change empathic interpretation materially, though the mental-health setting, privacy implications, and passive capture make transfer less straightforward.

Voice and binocular camera data are processed together, but camera data may be ambient context rather than a user-controlled input channel for the same operation. The quote provides neither a representative task nor a fusion example, so strong claims about impact or mechanism would be speculative.

Semantic and graphical inputs are explicitly combined to express one exploration intent. Dividing meaning and spatial form across channels is a strong authoring pattern with broad applicability, although the excerpt does not show the actual controls or system response.

Rough sketches and simple prompts jointly control a single image-generation request, with each channel carrying complementary spatial and semantic information. It addresses a genuine text-to-image control limitation, but by 2025 this is a well-populated design family.

Text and audio are used concurrently to search, modify, and create sounds, making fusion both explicit and operationally central. Using an example sound alongside language as a shared control signal is a less obvious and highly reusable multimodal move, even if demonstrated in synthesis.

Demonstrations and natural-language descriptions are accepted individually or together for the same data-wrangling interpretation. The mechanism generalizes widely and can reduce specification burden, but programming-by-demonstration plus language is established and the quote leaves capture details unstated.

The user sketches an idea and describes intent by voice, clearly providing complementary channels for one design request. It is a clean implementation, but it appears to be another product-design instance of the now-settled sketch-plus-speech prompting pattern.

Captured images plus voice, button, and dial prompts appear to feed one video-generation operation. The public-appliance setting and low-literacy physical controls make the modality mix socially and practically interesting, though the evidence does not explicitly describe fusion or channel switching.

Text, sketching, and region filling jointly support iterative world construction, cleanly embodying complementary channels within one authoring loop. As an early 2023 system, it helped articulate a now-common multimodal generative-authoring space and addresses both semantic and spatial control.

Voice and hand gestures support the same class of sterile imaging operations, but the excerpt does not establish whether they are fused or freely interchangeable. The sterile-first constraint makes modality choice load-bearing and potentially high-impact, although evidence of implementation and outcomes is limited.

Text, sketches, and reference images all contribute to character generation, directly supporting multimodal requests. The mechanism transfers to other visual-authoring domains, but it is a conventional combination of prompt channels and the quote gives little interaction detail.

The dual stream has a crisp division of labor: drawn frames specify pacing while keyword-emoji pairs specify atmosphere. This is a notably non-obvious multimodal composition that gives creators orthogonal controls, though its genre and comics framing limit direct transfer.

Speech, sketching, and direct manipulation coexist in embodied creation, strongly suggesting multimodal authoring. The quote does not demonstrate that the channels feed one request or remain interchangeable without modes, so representativeness and evidence are held below the strongest cases.

Selected text, sketches, images, and story context are explicitly analyzed together to generate one set of image-text cards. This is a strong fused-input instance with transferable co-editing logic, although its modality combination is less novel than the more distinctive candidates.
